{"id": "6:94/q25", "question": "What does bayn mean in this clause?", "turns_on": "Connection or separation, and whether connection is attested or inferred.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q25/p1", "position": "It means the bond or connection between them.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr, Khalīl, Zajjāj, Ibn Jinnī and others transmit the sense. Fārisī argues that a space between closely joined people becomes a metaphor for kinship, friendship and partnership; Samīn and Ālūsī defend the authorities against Ibn ʿAṭiyya's objection. Thaʿlabī and Baghawī call the word an opposite meaning term."}, {"id": "6:94/q25/p2", "position": "Its basic sense is separation or distance; severing that distance can be figurative.", "reasons": "Fārisī derives it from bāna, cites Abū Zayd's departing group and a hadith about what parts from a living thing. Ṭabrisī likewise gives the verbal noun. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says 'connection' lacks oral attestation, proposing figurative great distance; Abū Ḥayyān reports that analysis."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q26", "question": "How is baynakum read?", "turns_on": "Nominative baynukum, accusative baynakum, or mā baynakum.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q26/p1", "position": "Baynakum is accusative, usually an adverb with an understood bond or matter.", "reasons": "Nāfiʿ, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim are recurrently named; later sources add Abū Jaʿfar and a Medinan grouping. Ḥasan, Mujāhid and Abū Rajāʾ are also reported. Ṭabarī says both famous readings are sound; Qurṭubī and Biqāʿī say they agree in meaning."}, {"id": "6:94/q26/p2", "position": "Baynukum is nominative, making the bond a subject.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim are cited; most Meccan and Iraqi readers use it. Zajjāj prefers this reading, while Ṭabarī accepts both. Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar judged a dispute for the nominative; al-Aʿraj read it so."}, {"id": "6:94/q26/p3", "position": "A transmitted form reads mā baynakum, explicitly naming what was between them.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ prefers ʿAbd Allāh's idiom; Thaʿlabī attributes it to Ubayy and ʿAbd Allāh as well as some Medinan readers. Ibn ʿAṭiyya lists Ibn Masʿūd, Mujāhid and al-Aʿmash; Samīn uses it to support an omitted relative noun."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q27", "question": "How does taqaṭṭaʿa baynakum work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Nominative noun, retained accusative subject, omitted subject, verb competition, or verbal-noun subject.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q27/p1", "position": "In the accusative, an unspoken subject such as connection, affair or mā is severed; bayn is adverbial.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ calls mā baynakum more idiomatic. Fārisī infers waṣl from alleged partners; Sibawayh supplies contextual ellipsis. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Samīn call the account clear; Abū Ḥayyān objects that subjects cannot simply be omitted, while Samīn answers that a substitute can stand for it. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares a severed rope and 2:166."}, {"id": "6:94/q27/p2", "position": "In the nominative, bayn is an adverb used as a declinable noun and subject.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh, Fārisī, Abū ʿAlī and Samīn cite 41:5, 18:78, Sibawayh, Muhalhil, ʿAntara and poetry; Ṭabarī says accusative is more usual. Fārisī rejects taking it as the verbal noun 'separation' because severing separation reverses the sense. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it the meeting place used figuratively."}, {"id": "6:94/q27/p3", "position": "The accusative can retain adverbial form although bayn functions as subject.", "reasons": "Abū al-Ḥasan/Akhfash compares 60:3 and 72:11; Wāḥidī says frequent adverbial use preserves the accusative, while Samīn disputes frequency as a cause of indeclinability. Another account makes bayn indeclinable through annexation to an indeclinable word, with poetry on mithl, ghayr and maqāla."}, {"id": "6:94/q27/p4", "position": "The two verbs compete for their shared subject, the alleged idols or claims.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān prefers the later verb ḍalla governing it and taqaṭṭaʿa taking a pronoun. Samīn reports Basran later-verb and Kufan earlier-verb analyses, assigning mā accordingly."}, {"id": "6:94/q27/p5", "position": "Taqaṭṭaʿa can be predicated of its verbal noun, meaning severance occurred.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī gives this paraphrase; the Shaykh objects that 'severing severed' has no distinct predicate and could imply reunion. Samīn replies that the paraphrase is interpretive; Ālūsī and Safāqisī defend the distinct definite noun and indefinite verb, comparing 12:35."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q28", "question": "What bond or relation is severed, and when?", "turns_on": "Worldly social ties, ties to idols, or soul and body; afterlife versus present world.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q28/p1", "position": "Worldly kinship, affection, support and mutual contact among people end at judgment.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Mujāhid, Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh give ties, with Ibn ʿAbbās adding homes. Baghawī cites 2:166. Durr reports ʿUmar's marriage to Umm Kulthūm and the saying that all lineage and bond ends except the Prophet's."}, {"id": "6:94/q28/p2", "position": "The link between idolaters and their claimed deities or intercessors is broken.", "reasons": "Muqātil names affection with angelic partners; Ḍaḥḥāk says the bond with gods. Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly includes both groups in the pronoun. Abū Ḥayyān cites 2:166, and Ṭabāṭabāʾ compares Iblīs disowning followers at 14:22 and 10:28."}, {"id": "6:94/q28/p3", "position": "In Rāzī's account, the soul's connection with the body is irrecoverably severed.", "reasons": "Rāzī links this to acute grief when certainty makes recovery impossible; Abū Ḥayyān objects that the verse does not express that meaning."}, {"id": "6:94/q28/p4", "position": "The verse can refer to a bond already disappearing in this world.", "reasons": "Māwardī attributes this possibility to Mujāhid, as opposed to a broken gathering in the afterlife."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q29", "question": "What is lost in 'what you used to claim'?", "turns_on": "Vanished idols or intercession, denial of resurrection, false assertions, or idols unable to find worshippers.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q29/p1", "position": "The supposed idols and intercessors, with their promised aid, vanish or prove void.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī says they cannot even locate their gods; Ibn Kathīr cites many scenes of idols, followers and allies disowning one another. Bursawī says they cannot avert punishment. Asad identifies imagined mediators. Ibn ʿĀshūr's sharper reading is that idols themselves cannot find their worshippers to intercede."}, {"id": "6:94/q29/p2", "position": "Their false claims generally have disappeared or been exposed as lies.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says what they used to lie about is gone; Wāḥidī and Qurṭubī stress false worldly assertions. Ibn ʿAṭiyya glosses ḍalla as vanished and gone."}, {"id": "6:94/q29/p3", "position": "Their claim that there would be no resurrection or recompense is shown false.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Bayḍāwī offer this as an alternative to the intercession claim."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q30", "question": "How is the final mā kuntum tazʿumūn constructed?", "turns_on": "Relative/descriptive mā with omitted objects versus verbal-noun mā.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q30/p1", "position": "Mā is relative or descriptive, with omitted objects of tazʿumūn recovered as idols and their intercession.", "reasons": "Samīn says both objects are elided for concision, citing a poem on omitted object of taḥsab; Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr recover them from context. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers mā referring to useless idols."}, {"id": "6:94/q30/p2", "position": "Mā is verbal-noun-forming, referring to their claim itself.", "reasons": "Samīn says the second object still needs supplying; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others on this reading but prefers the idols' loss of way."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q31", "question": "What remains with a person at death and in the grave?", "turns_on": "Deeds and knowledge can accompany the believer, while worldly companions fail.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q31/p1", "position": "Knowledge of God, righteous deeds and taqwā accompany the believer, unlike worldly possessions.", "reasons": "Rāzī says sound knowledge and virtue remain in grave and resurrection. Bursawī names testimony, prayer, fasting and remembrance as four grave companions, and reports good deeds protecting and brightening the grave while evil deeds torment. Saʿdī's verses say grief and joy pass but deeds and good name remain. A Yemeni grave vision presents a black dog as the person's deeds and Yā Sīn with companion sūras as protection."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q32", "question": "How do inward readers describe the end of the journey?", "turns_on": "Whether perceived independent entities vanish or the seeker passes beyond all supports.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q32/p1", "position": "At unity, independent entities and causal supports are seen to have no separate influence.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says supposed entities vanish when everything is witnessed in God. Bursawī traces tajrīd, tafrīd and tawḥīd to divine majesty; Gabriel stopped at the Lote Tree, and primordial care alone lets the seeker pass the known station of 37:164."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q33", "question": "What does the return to God reveal about power and dependence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q33/p1", "position": "God alone governs people; worldly causes have no independent efficacy, and death exposes this.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾ says apparent causes act only by God's measure and that bodily separation removes material supports. The next verses explain the causes as God's managed creations. Qāshānī's inward reading likewise sees claimed separate entities vanish. Iṣlāḥī says abilities were grants testing gratitude."}]}

Elmalılı urges imagining the reckoning and avoiding injustice. Ṭabrisī urges obedience that saves."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q35", "question": "What occasion or audience is reported for the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether al-Naḍr's saying is a specific occasion or an example of a general challenge.", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q35/p1", "position": "Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith claimed al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā would intercede for him, prompting the verse.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima's report recurs in Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Durr, Suyūṭī, and Ālūsī. Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes no grade. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows mockery or ignorance but denies a discrete occasion."}, {"id": "6:94/q35/p2", "position": "The rebuke concerns idol worshippers generally.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī reports all idol worshippers' claim; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says most Arabs sought nearness through idols, excluding those recognizing no other deity. Bursawī names Quraysh and their boast of wealth and children; Iṣlāḥī notes the shift from People of the Book to Meccan idolaters."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q36", "question": "How does 6:94 connect with its surrounding passage and sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q36/p1", "position": "Other verses echo solitary return, broken bonds and idols' failure.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī links 7:29–30 to 6:94; Baghawī and Abū Ḥayyān cite 2:166; Ibn Kathīr lists 2:166–167, 23:101, 29:25, 28:64, 6:22–24 and 26:92–93. Study Quran compares 19:95 and scenes of false powers disowning followers."}, {"id": "6:94/q36/p2", "position": "It makes judgment vivid after the death scene, closing a monotheism discussion before the sūra turns to God's created signs.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the previous passage answers deniers of the dead's awareness and shows angels seizing them; he links the opening angels to final judgment. Ibn ʿĀshūr coordinates this with 6:93 and calls it a rebuke of resurrection denial. Iṣlāḥī sees the next section arguing from the world for monotheism, prophethood and hereafter, within the sūra's recurring themes."}]}
{"id": "6:94/q37", "question": "What does the related discussion say about Qur'anic bal?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:94/q37/p1", "position": "Bal may retract and correct, as well as mark a transition.", "reasons": "Burhān rejects al-Basīṭ's and Ibn Mālik's claim that Qur'anic bal only marks transition."}]}
{"id": "7:11/q01", "question": "What force does وَلَقَدْ add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q01/p1", "position": "It emphatically asserts the creation account, with an implied oath.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies lām and qad as reinforcing the report like 7:10; al-Sāmarrāʾī also identifies an implied oath and notes al-Aʿrāf’s stronger opening than Ṣād."}]}
{"id": "7:11/q02", "question": "What does خَلَقْنَٰكُمْ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether creation denotes actual origination, initial design, or determination.", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q02/p1", "position": "God brought into existence or prepared the first substance of humanity according to measure.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives measured origination and also creation without a prior model; Ṭabrisī links measure to wisdom; Ibn ʿĀshūr defines bringing into existence. Biqāʿī describes preparation of material with capacity for form; Elmalılı begins before any individual existed."}, {"id": "7:11/q02/p2", "position": "It denotes design or determination before the final form.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says khalaqa alone covers consequences but alongside taṣwīr narrows to initial design. Rāzī uses divine decree and will; his preferred account sets the forms in the Preserved Tablet before Adam."}, {"id": "7:11/q02/p3", "position": "It denotes the first, unformed stage of bodily and species development.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu describes ordering chaos into form and embryonic, bodily, intellectual development; Asad describes embryonic and evolutionary development."}]}
{"id": "7:11/q03", "question": "What does صَوَّرْنَٰكُمْ add to creation?", "turns_on": "Whether form is bodily shape, final perfection, or prior potential.", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q03/p1", "position": "God gave a thing its visible bodily structure and distinct human shape.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabrisī define taṣwīr as giving outward form; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares shaping clay. Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes bringing into existence from giving particular human form; Qur'an Yolu says form and shape."}, {"id": "7:11/q03/p2", "position": "It marks the final form and perfection following initial design.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī contrasts initial design with final perfection; Ibn ʿĀshūr sees imaging as a higher perfection involving refined perception and deliberation, comparing 23:14."}, {"id": "7:11/q03/p3", "position": "It refers to a prepared capacity for a future form.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī compares clay able to grow a tree and reconciles Ṣād's actual formation with this verse's preparatory capacity. He reads a forty-two-night embryonic formation report as such preparation within the second forty-day period."}]}
{"id": "7:11/q04", "question": "Who is created and fashioned, and where or when?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural names Adam representatively, descendants at a primordial stage, womb development, or prior decree.", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q04/p1", "position": "Both verbs concern Adam: God created him, then gave him form before commanding prostration.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites Adam's creation from dust (3:59); Zamakhsharī, Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, and Ālūsī invoke the next command. Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr prefer this sequence; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the transition concise. Some supply 'your father'; al-Ḥasan and Yūsuf al-Naḥwī favor it. Adam was first unformed clay; Eve from his rib appears in al-Zajjāj’s account."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p2", "position": "Adam was created and the descendants were fashioned in his back or loins before the command.", "reasons": "Mujāhid’s reports describe descendants as particles, sometimes connected with their eventual reward; Abū ʿUbayd prefers this due to the sequel. Ṭabrisī and Ālūsī report Ibn ʿAbbās and others. The primordial covenant in 7:172 is cited; variants phrase creation as occurring in Adam’s back."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p3", "position": "People were created in men's or fathers' loins and fashioned in women's or mothers' wombs.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Aʿmash and others transmit this. Ibn al-Sāʾib specifies male and female reproductive fluids joining; one report from Ibn ʿAbbās via Saʿīd b. Jubayr was graded sound by al-Ḥākim, as Ibn Kathīr reports."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p4", "position": "Adam was created, and his descendants were fashioned afterward in wombs or as successive generations.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk are repeatedly transmitted. Qatāda specifies clay, clot, lump, bones, flesh and a new creation; Muqātil notes sex, color and bodily variation. Qurṭubī cites 23:12–13, 4:1 while allowing multiple views."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p5", "position": "Each person is created in the womb and then fashioned there with hearing, sight, fingers or other organs.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī, Maʿmar, Yamān and other reports specify opening sensory faculties and fingers. This reading generates the question of how the ensuing command can follow descendant formation."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p6", "position": "People were created in Adam's back, then fashioned in wombs.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is transmitted through ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ḥārith and elsewhere; ʿAṭāʾ also gives this allocation. It differs from placing both acts in Adam's back."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p7", "position": "God created the spirits, then fashioned the bodies.", "reasons": "Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā supplies omitted 'spirits' and 'bodies'; Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān also transmit this distinction."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p8", "position": "The words describe the development of the human species and each individual from initial formless matter to completed form.", "reasons": "Elmalılı includes clay and seed in fathers’ loins, with Adam representing the species; Asad includes embryo and evolution; Kur'an Yolu prefers collective species development, including intellectual maturity."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p9", "position": "People were created in Adam's back and fashioned as particles at the primordial covenant.", "reasons": "Bāghawī gives this view; Mujāhid’s account is judged best by al-Naḥḥās, who cites 7:172. Qurṭubī reports the covenant hadith."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p10", "position": "Adam and Eve were created and then formed as the two parents.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says Adam was from earth and Eve from his rib; al-Zajjāj also notes Eve's rib and shaping."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p11", "position": "God created your spouses, then fashioned your bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn attributes this unusual interpretation to Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p12", "position": "Creation is God's prior determination, and fashioning is the inscription of future forms in the Preserved Tablet.", "reasons": "Rāzī calls this closer than alternatives: after decree and inscription God actually created Adam and commanded prostration."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p13", "position": "Adam was created and formed in Paradise, and descendants were formed in his loins at the covenant.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān transmits this as a chronological report from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "7:11/q04/p14", "position": "God intended to create and fashion humanity, stated prospectively before Adam's actual creation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares prospective wording in the angels' report before Lot's departure (51:35)."}]}
{"id": "7:11/q05", "question": "Why is humanity addressed in the plural when Adam is named?", "turns_on": "Whether ancestry licenses representative addre

ss or the address literally includes the species.", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q05/p1", "position": "An ancestor's creation and honor can be attributed to descendants, since Adam is their origin.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī compares 2:63; Ṭabrisī and Rāzī likewise cite ancestral covenant language. Ibn Kathīr compares 2:57; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 69:11. A tribal poem about Dhī Qār illustrates speaking to descendants about ancestors. Some explain plural by Adam as leader or an honorific plural."}, {"id": "7:11/q05/p2", "position": "The address directly encompasses the whole human race, with Adam its representative and bearer of its potential traits.", "reasons": "Elmalılı and Kur'an Yolu make Adam the species’ exemplar; Asad says Adam symbolizes humanity. Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects bare kinship as enough to transfer Adam’s creation to descendants, because the verse names Adam for prostration."}, {"id": "7:11/q05/p3", "position": "The immediate addressees are Quraysh or polytheists within a universal human address.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī specifies Quraysh and their ordained trials; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the address covers all humanity but especially the polytheists targeted by the sūra."}]}
{"id": "7:11/q06", "question": "What does each ثُمَّ express, and how does the order work?", "turns_on": "How to reconcile human formation with the earlier command to prostrate.", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q06/p1", "position": "Here ثم may function like و, coordinating without chronological delay.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash adduces a father-and-mother poetic line; al-Zajjāj and Basran grammarians reject the analogy, while Bāghawī reports it for both particles."}, {"id": "7:11/q06/p2", "position": "It marks real temporal succession: Adam was created, formed, and then the angels were commanded.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī rejects metrical poetic ثم = و and unsupported inversion; al-Zajjāj appeals to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh. Zamakhsharī, Nasafī and others use the following command to identify Adam; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says early readings retain interval. Ālūsī distinguishes an earlier conditional order in 15:29 from the enacted command after formation."}, {"id": "7:11/q06/p3", "position": "The later ثم orders the telling: after describing humanity, God tells them about His prior command.", "reasons": "ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā and al-Sīrāfī endorse narrative order; Abū Ḥayyān calls it easier for an all-human address. Al-Samīn calls the version with both particles narrative order of little explanatory gain; Ibn ʿAṭiyya applies this to womb formation."}, {"id": "7:11/q06/p4", "position": "The statement is reordered: Adam was created, prostration commanded, and descendants then fashioned.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, Māwardī, Baghawī and Qurṭubī report fronting and postponement; Ṭabarī rejects it without contextual evidence."}, {"id": "7:11/q06/p5", "position": "ثم can mark rise in rank rather than elapsed time.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭībī ranks Adam’s honor through angelic prostration above his creation, connected with knowledge in 2:31; Ibn ʿĀshūr ranks both human imaging and prostration above preceding stages; al-Zarkashī allows non-temporal progression in qualities."}, {"id": "7:11/q06/p6", "position": "The sequence can include gradual initial and final formation across Adam and each person.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī reports Adam’s beginning in clay and every person's beginning in a drop (23:13). Biqāʿī reads preparation of a form before its realization; the embryo reports of forty and forty-two days are reconciled on that basis."}, {"id": "7:11/q06/p7", "position": "The first ثم is chronological but the second marks narrative order.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn lists the mixed explanation; he also reports first-clause Adam and second-clause descendants within that family of readings."}]}
{"id": "7:11/q07", "question": "How is مَلَٰٓئِكَةِ analyzed linguistically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q07/p1", "position": "Its form is analyzed as مفاعلة or معافلة; malak commonly drops an original hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya refers to earlier derivation in al-Baqara; Sībawayh cites malʾak, maʾlaka and malʾaka for 'message' while noting common hamza loss."}]}
{"id": "7:11/q08", "question": "Which angels were commanded to bow?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite plural denotes every angel, those present on earth, or another group.", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q08/p1", "position": "All angels were addressed and bowed.", "reasons": "Bursevī says general wording lacks a restricting proof; Biqāʿī includes angels of heaven and earth; Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 15:30. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows all but says the generic article alone does not require it."}, {"id": "7:11/q08/p2", "position": "The angels on earth or present where Adam was created were addressed.", "reasons": "Muqātil includes Iblis among the earthly group; Abū al-ʿĀliya reports earthly angels; some argue heavenly angels bow only to God. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Ibn ʿAbbās on those present."}, {"id": "7:11/q08/p3", "position": "The angels of the heavens and Throne were addressed.", "reasons": "Rāzī records this side of the dispute without choosing."}, {"id": "7:11/q08/p4", "position": "The angels represent forces of nature.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports Süleyman Ateş’s proposal."}, {"id": "7:11/q08/p5", "position": "The evidence does not fix which angels bowed.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu prefers restraint because this unseen matter has no sound transmitted proof."}]}

{"id": "7:11/q17", "question": "What is the syntax and force of لَمْ يَكُن مِّنَ ٱلسَّٰجِدِينَ?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is independent or circumstantial, and whether it adds force to the exception.", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q17/p1", "position": "It emphatically restates the exception and strengthens denial.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports emphatic restatement; Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'not among the prostrators' is stronger than 'did not prostrate' (6:56). {"id": "7:11/q24", "question": "Which supplied notes discuss other subjects without interpreting 7:11?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:11/q24/p1", "position": "These notes concern separate Arabic grammar, history, hadith, rhetoric, and recitation topics; they make no claim about the meaning of this verse.", "reasons": "Sībawayh’s #623, #598, #788, #605, #608, and #603 treat weak-letter diminutives, hamza substitutions and inversions, plurals, deletions and analogical forms; #69 treats apposition, partitives, predicates, circumstances and object slots, with examples from 3:97, 7:75, 2:251, 8:37 and poetry. Majāz glosses extra lā in 7:12; al-Zajjāj disputes a hamza derivation of maṣāʾib. Ibn Hishām recounts Lakhniʿa and Dhū Nuwās, rival Quraysh genealogies and q-r-sh etymologies, and the Trench; al-Azraqī collects Black Stone origins, colors, healings and Last Day testimony. Ibn Ḥibbān records al-Rumayṣāʾ in Paradise and the virtues of Prophetic knowledge. Al-Bāqillānī debates the Quran's intrinsic inimitability against ṣarfa; al-Jurjānī analyzes transferred senses, exception and restriction, and whether new wording can claim an old meaning; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ critiques al-Bāqillānī’s method. Al-Nashr records hadith chains, hamza easing, reading routes, and the benefits of multiple readings; al-Itqān treats accepted reading conditions, the ten readers, and suitable recitation amounts. One Ṭabāṭabāʾī note disputes an unsupported consensus on jinn and angels as mutable airy bodies. None of these notes supplies an answer about the wording or events of 7:11."}]}

{"id": "7:12/q04", "question": "How does 'allā tasjuda' express the reason for Iblis's refusal?", "turns_on": "Whether lā contributes negation, reinforces the rebuke, or is accommodated by ellipsis or a different sense of manaʿa.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q04/p1", "position": "Lā is an emphatic or connective addition; the question means 'what prevented you from prostrating?'.", "reasons": "Farra, Akhfash, Zajjaj and others compare 21:95, 57:29, 6:109, 75:1, 90:1, and 38:75, where the question lacks lā. Alusi says the accounts differ little."}, {"id": "7:12/q04/p4", "position": "Manaʿa means forbade, ordered, or told; the question asks who told Iblis not to prostrate.", "reasons": "Some Basrans and Thaʿlab say speech can prevent action; Wāḥidī also attributes a version to Farrā. {"id": "7:12/q08", "question": "What legal force does the command and Iblis's rebuke show?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q08/p1", "position": "An unqualified divine command entails obligation.", "reasons": "Zajjaj distinguishes denying an obligation, which is unbelief, from Adam and Eve's confessed and repented sin; Iblis's defiance was disbelief. {"id": "7:12/q09", "question": "How does 'I am better than him' answer the question?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison is treated as an elliptical answer or a diversion from the charge.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q09/p1", "position": "It answers indirectly: Iblis's presumed superiority is the reason he would not bow.", "reasons": "Farra contrasts a grammatically matched reply; Wahidi's Abu Bakr compares answering 'whose house?' with 'its owner is Zayd'. Tabari says Iblis boasts instead of directly naming the obstacle. Tabatabai says the fronted 'I' foregrounds ego; Burhan notes an objection that it answers a different question."}, {"id": "7:12/q09/p2", "position": "Iblis diverts to a separate comparison that cannot excuse his disobedience.", "reasons": "Burhan's reply to the objection says he shifted to an unanswerable issue; Elmalili says he argued back instead of confessing and apologizing."}]}
{"id": "7:12/q10", "question": "Why did Iblis refuse to prostrate?", "turns_on": "Whether the refusal is explained by his stated material ranking, the pride beneath it, or his use of that ranking against command.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q10/p1", "position": "He believed himself superior because fire was nobler than Adam's clay and a superior should not bow to an inferior.", "reasons": "Muqatil says fire overcomes clay. Ibn Abbas reports Iblis also claimed to be older and stronger; fire is said to rise, shine, act and convey life, while clay is heavy, dark and receptive. Razi reports the analogy with leading jurists serving a lesser one. Elmalili calls the premises concealed sophistry."}, {"id": "7:12/q10/p2", "position": "Arrogance, envy, and self-regard made him refuse and exposed prior insincerity.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says the intent was concealed before Adam's formation and surfaced when angels bowed; Qushayri says earlier service was not sincere. Qatada calls pride and envy the beginning of sins. Islahi says jealousy at humanity's preference fueled later hostility; Elmalili says the first conflict of command and desire revealed self-service."}, {"id": "7:12/q10/p3", "position": "He reasoned from personal analogy against God's explicit command.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Qurtubi cite Ibn Abbas that obedience should precede analogy. Baydawi calls this the origin of arrogant rational moral judgment. Elmalili says a true material contrast was joined to false premises; Tabatabai says the real contest was with God's majesty."}, {"id": "7:12/q10/p4", "position": "In an inward reading, seeing one's own substance and worship displaced reliance on the Bestower.", "reasons": "Sulami's Wasiti says claiming 'I' through ritual practice itself is ruinous; Ibn Ata says self-regard veils reverence for God. Qushayri says merit is God's allotment and a claimed independent rank encroaches on lordship."}]}
{"id": "7:12/q11", "question": "Does fire's origin make Iblis better than Adam?", "turns_on": "Whether raw elements rank created persons, whether earth has the better qualities, and what standard gives created beings merit.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q11/p1", "position": "Iblis claims fire's light, purity, force, subtlety and upward movement make him superior.", "reasons": "Muqatil adds that fire overcomes clay; Razi adds warmth ripening fruit and growth, against cold age. These are presented as Iblis's premise by the sources, not their verdict."}, {"id": "7:12/q11/p2", "position": "Clay or earth has stronger claims to excellence than fire.", "reasons": "Tabari, Qaffal and others contrast clay's gravity, patience, stability, modesty and receptivity to repentance with fire's rashness, pride and destructiveness; Tabari adds prior divine decree. Clay gathers and sustains plants, earth supports habitation, food and purification. Thaʿlabi and Qurtubi cite Paradise's musk soil, no reported Paradise fire or Hell soil, fire as punishment, and fire's need for earth as a place. Tabarsi defines this as practical benefit, not reward for inert matter; Qurtubi cites 39:16; Study Quran cites 4:43 and 5:6. Ibn Atiyya questions Tabari's trait inference."}, {"id": "7:12/q11/p3", "position": "Material origin cannot by itself establish a creature's rank; God-given form, deeds, purpose and end decide it.", "reasons": "Razi says God brings believers from unbelievers and vice versa; a believing Abyssinian exceeds an unbelieving Qurashi. Ibn Atiyya says both materials are inert and Adam's spirit is not clay; Abu Hayyan and Alusi use similar arguments, the latter adding thorn-tree fruit and a bulb's flower. Biqai judges by end, Tabatabai by divine care; Ibn Ashur stresses arrangement and capacities. Elmalili says both are equally created; Kuranyolu calls disobedience unjustified."}]}
{"id": "7:12/q12", "question": "What special honor to Adam did Iblis's material comparison overlook?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q12/p1", "position": "God formed Adam specially, breathed His spirit into him, taught him, made him vicegerent, and commanded prostration in his honor.", "reasons": "Tabari lists creation by God's hand, spirit, names and angelic prostration; Baydawi adds form and purpose. Islahi and Alusi say bowing at God's command was ultimately to God, not a shameful service to an inferior."}, {"id": "7:12/q12/p2", "position": "Adam's honor follows God's choice and wisdom, not any entitlement of his material.", "reasons": "Qushayri assigns superiority to God's allotment; Tabarsi says obedience follows divine wisdom and servants' interests. {"id": "7:12/q13", "question": "What do the fire and clay origins imply about Iblis and created beings?", "turns_on": "Whether the stated materials are literal origins, dominant constituents, or read inwardly as faculties.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q13/p1", "position": "The origins are real; Iblis is a created jinn associated with fire, Adam with clay.", "reasons": "Mujahid says Iblis's descendants were made from water. Tabatabai says later state and detailed creation are undisclosed and possibly differ from first existence; Asad points to 38:76."}, {"id": "7:12/q13/p2", "position": "The elements may be dominant constituents rather than the whole physical composition.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Alusi suggest clay and fire predominate in bodies made of several elements; Ibn Ashur says clay includes life-supporting water and fire has material rays."}, {"id": "7:12/q13/p3", "position": "The passage supports generation, corruption and the bodily creation of Iblis and devils.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Alusi derive the changing composition of originated bodies, against pre-eternal spirits."}, {"id": "7:12/q13/p4", "position": "The imaginative faculty is the inward Iblis, tied to the fiery animal spirit.", "reasons": "Qashani locates it in vaporous humors ascending from heart to brain; heat fosters elevation.
